cases.title: Sharps Safety and Needle Stick Exposure
cases.stem: A nurse finishes giving a subcutaneous injection during a hectic morning round. As another alarm sounds, the nurse reflexively attempts to recap the used needle before disposal. The needle slips and punctures the glove and skin of the nurse’s finger. The nurse immediately feels embarrassed and wonders whether the injury is too small to report. However, the source patient’s bloodborne pathogen status is not yet fully known. The event requires correct exposure response and reinforces why recapping sharps is unsafe.

questions.title: Recognise cues
questions.stem: Which elements make this a significant sharps safety incident? Select all that apply.

options.text: A used needle punctured the nurse’s skin
The needle was being recapped
The patient’s bloodborne risk status may be unknown
The injury occurred during a distracted workflow moment
Reporting and follow-up may be needed

questions.rationale: All of these details matter. Recapping is a known sharps hazard, and even a small puncture requires appropriate exposure management.

questions.title: Analyse cues
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: Small needle sticks can be ignored if the glove was on
This is an occupational exposure requiring immediate first aid, reporting, and follow-up according to policy
Only the employee’s supervisor needs to know next week
Recapping is acceptable if done carefully

questions.rationale: Gloves reduce but do not eliminate risk. The nurse must treat this as a reportable exposure and follow policy promptly.

questions.title: Prioritise hypothesis
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Risk for bloodborne pathogen exposure related to sharps injury
Disturbed sleep pattern
Embarrassment about the incident
Delay in lunch break

questions.rationale: The priority is exposure management and prevention of infection-related harm.

questions.title: Take action
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Perform immediate first aid, report the exposure promptly, and follow occupational health or exposure protocol
Hide the injury because it seems minor
Continue working without telling anyone
Recap the needle more carefully next time and do nothing else

questions.rationale: Immediate first aid and reporting are required. Delayed or hidden exposure increases risk and weakens safety culture.

questions.title: Advanced decision
questions.stem: Which additional safety actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Review sharps disposal practices and avoid recapping
Complete required documentation and source/exposed-person follow-up steps
Participate in system review if workflow contributed to the incident
Reinforce use of puncture-resistant sharps containers nearby
Assume near-misses and minor injuries do not matter

questions.rationale: These are all appropriate. Safety culture depends on learning from both injuries and near-misses.

questions.title: Evaluate outcomes
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective management?

options.text: The exposure is addressed promptly, follow-up is completed, and safer sharps handling is reinforced
The injury is hidden and no protocol is followed
Recapping continues because the staff are busy
Documentation is avoided to protect reputations

questions.rationale: Effective management protects staff, supports legal and occupational requirements, and prevents recurrence.

cases.title: Oxygen Therapy and Fire Hazard
cases.stem: Mr. Luke Bennett, a 69-year-old patient with COPD, is receiving oxygen via nasal cannula. The nurse notices that he is using petroleum-based lip ointment and that his daughter has plugged in a small electric heating device near the bed because he says the room feels cold. The oxygen tubing runs loosely across the linens. The patient says no one told him the lip ointment or electrical setup could be dangerous. The nurse recognises a serious environmental safety hazard in an oxygen-enriched setting.

questions.title: Recognise cues
questions.stem: Which factors create fire or burn risk in this scenario? Select all that apply.

options.text: Oxygen therapy in use
Petroleum-based product near the face
Electrical heating device near the bed
Loose oxygen tubing near linens and equipment
Lack of patient education about oxygen safety

questions.rationale: All of these factors increase hazard in an oxygen-enriched environment. Oxygen supports combustion, petroleum products are unsafe near oxygen, and electrical heat sources add risk.

questions.title: Analyse cues
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: The setup is safe because oxygen itself does not burn
The patient is at increased risk of fire or burn injury and requires immediate environmental safety correction
Lip ointment choice is only a comfort issue
Electrical devices are always safe if the patient is awake

questions.rationale: Although oxygen is not itself flammable, it greatly increases combustion risk. The setup requires immediate correction.

questions.title: Prioritise hypothesis
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Risk for fire-related injury in an oxygen-enriched environment
Disturbed sleep pattern
Mild discomfort from dry lips
Knowledge deficit about nutrition

questions.rationale: The immediate threat is environmental fire or burn injury.

questions.title: Take action
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Remove the unsafe items, correct the environment immediately, and educate the patient and family about oxygen precautions
Wait until discharge teaching to mention oxygen safety
Ignore the petroleum product because it is only on the lips
Turn the oxygen up higher to compensate for the room setup

questions.rationale: Safety hazards should be corrected immediately, not later. Oxygen safety education is part of risk reduction.

questions.title: Advanced decision
questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Ensure only approved water-based products are used if needed
Keep ignition sources away from oxygen equipment
Secure tubing to reduce tangling and environmental hazard
Reinforce no-smoking and fire-risk education as appropriate
Assume family members already know oxygen safety rules

questions.rationale: These are all correct safety interventions. Education should never be assumed.

questions.title: Evaluate outcomes
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective management?

options.text: Unsafe products and devices are removed, the patient understands oxygen precautions, and the environment is safer
The heating device remains because the family prefers it
Oxygen tubing stays tangled across the bed
Education is omitted because no fire has occurred yet

questions.rationale: Preventing harm is the goal. A safer environment and improved understanding show effective nursing intervention.

cases.title: Aspiration Risk After Stroke
cases.stem: Mr. Victor Singh, a 77-year-old man recovering from an acute stroke, is awaiting formal swallow assessment. A family member tries to help by offering water while he is semi-reclined in bed. The patient coughs forcefully, his voice sounds wet afterward, and he appears distressed. The nurse recognises that the patient may have dysphagia and that aspiration prevention is critical. The situation requires immediate assessment, education, and safe feeding precautions.

questions.title: Recognise cues
questions.stem: Which findings suggest aspiration risk? Select all that apply.

options.text: Recent stroke
No completed swallow assessment yet
Water given while semi-reclined
Coughing during swallowing
Wet voice afterward

questions.rationale: All listed cues suggest dysphagia and aspiration risk. Stroke can impair swallowing, and coughing with a wet voice after intake is especially concerning.

questions.title: Analyse cues
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: The patient tolerated fluids well
The patient may have aspirated and needs immediate swallowing safety intervention
Coughing always means the airway is cleared and there is no problem
Family feeding before assessment is harmless

questions.rationale: The nurse must take the event seriously. Aspiration may lead to airway compromise or pneumonia if precautions are not applied.

questions.title: Prioritise hypothesis
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Risk for aspiration and impaired airway protection
Disturbed sleep pattern
Social isolation
Low self-esteem

questions.rationale: Airway protection comes first in a patient with suspected swallowing impairment.

questions.title: Take action
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Stop oral intake, assess the patient’s respiratory status, position safely, and ensure formal swallowing precautions are followed
Offer more water to test tolerance
Leave the family to continue helping because they mean well
Delay assessment until meal time

questions.rationale: The nurse must stop unsafe oral intake and protect the airway immediately. Family intention does not change the aspiration risk.

questions.title: Advanced decision
questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Maintain upright positioning during any allowed intake
Clarify NPO status and swallow orders with the team
Educate the family about why unapproved oral intake is unsafe
Monitor for coughing, choking, wet voice, or respiratory change
Assume aspiration risk ends once the coughing stops

questions.rationale: All these actions are appropriate. Aspiration complications may continue even after immediate coughing subsides.

questions.title: Evaluate outcomes
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective management?

options.text: Oral intake is withheld until safe, aspiration signs do not recur, and the family understands swallowing precautions
Water continues to be offered because the patient is thirsty
The patient develops worsening respiratory symptoms without reassessment
Positioning is ignored during future meals

questions.rationale: Effective care prevents repeat aspiration and improves family understanding of safety precautions.

cases.title: Pressure Injury Prevention in an Immobile Patient
cases.stem: Mrs. Janet Clarke is a 68-year-old patient with limited mobility after a stroke. She requires assistance for turning and has poor nutritional intake due to fatigue. During a busy shift, repositioning is delayed several times. By evening, the nurse notices non-blanching redness over the sacral area and mild skin warmth. The nurse recognises early pressure injury development and understands that prevention is safer and far easier than treatment. The situation requires immediate protective action and reassessment of the turning plan.

questions.title: Recognise cues
questions.stem: Which findings indicate increased pressure injury risk or early injury? Select all that apply.

options.text: Immobility after stroke
Repositioning delays
Poor nutritional intake
Non-blanching redness over sacrum
Warmth at pressure area

questions.rationale: All listed findings are relevant. Immobility, delayed turning, poor nutrition, and early skin changes are classic pressure injury concerns.

questions.title: Analyse cues
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: The skin changes are insignificant and can be reviewed later
Early pressure injury is developing and immediate prevention/escalation measures are required
Warm skin means circulation is fine and there is no issue
Pressure injuries occur only in ICU patients

questions.rationale: The patient is showing early pressure damage. Prompt intervention can prevent progression.

questions.title: Prioritise hypothesis
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Risk for worsening tissue injury related to sustained pressure and impaired mobility
Disturbed sleep
Social withdrawal
Need for reading materials

questions.rationale: Tissue preservation is the immediate priority. Delay may convert an early injury into a deeper wound.

questions.title: Take action
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Relieve pressure immediately, reposition the patient, assess the skin thoroughly, and update the prevention plan
Massage the reddened area vigorously
Leave the patient in the same position until morning
Cover the area without reassessment

questions.rationale: Pressure must be relieved immediately. Vigorous massage can worsen tissue damage and is not appropriate.

questions.title: Advanced decision
questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Use pressure-relieving surfaces or devices as indicated
Strengthen repositioning schedules and staff communication
Address nutrition and moisture management
Document skin findings precisely
Assume redness will resolve without follow-up

questions.rationale: All these are core pressure injury prevention measures. Accurate documentation and regular reassessment are essential.

questions.title: Evaluate outcomes
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective management?

options.text: Pressure is relieved, skin is monitored closely, the area does not worsen, and preventive measures are consistently maintained
Redness deepens while repositioning remains inconsistent
Nutrition is ignored because skin care alone is enough
Documentation is skipped

questions.rationale: Effective management prevents progression and supports whole-patient pressure injury prevention.

cases.title: Infusion Pump Alarm and Equipment Safety
cases.stem: A patient on IV fluids and vasoactive support has an infusion pump that alarms repeatedly during the night shift. Because the alarm has sounded several times earlier for minor occlusion issues, a fatigued nurse silences it twice without immediately checking the line and pump settings. Shortly afterward, the patient becomes more short of breath and develops worsening blood pressure instability. When the nurse finally checks the equipment, the infusion settings are incorrect and the IV line is partially occluded. The scenario highlights the danger of alarm fatigue and failure to assess equipment safety promptly.

questions.title: Recognise cues
questions.stem: Which factors make this a serious equipment safety event? Select all that apply.

options.text: Repeated pump alarms
Silencing the alarm without full assessment
Incorrect infusion settings later discovered
Partial line occlusion
Patient deterioration occurring during the delay

questions.rationale: All of these factors contribute to a serious safety event. Alarm fatigue is dangerous because it may delay recognition of true equipment malfunction or medication error.

questions.title: Analyse cues
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: Pump alarms can usually be ignored if they happen often
Repeated alarms require direct assessment because unresolved equipment issues can rapidly harm patients
Only biomedical engineering is responsible for infusion safety
Patient symptoms are probably unrelated to the pump

questions.rationale: Nurses must assess alarms directly rather than assuming they are routine nuisances. Infusion pumps deliver high-risk therapy and incorrect settings can quickly cause harm.

questions.title: Prioritise hypothesis
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Risk for medication or fluid harm due to faulty infusion delivery
Disturbed sleep pattern caused by alarms
Staff annoyance
Mild paperwork delay

questions.rationale: The immediate concern is patient harm from incorrect infusion delivery, particularly with vasoactive or other critical fluids.

questions.title: Take action
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Assess the patient and infusion system immediately, correct the equipment issue safely, and escalate as needed based on the patient’s condition
Silence the alarm again and observe from the doorway
Turn off the pump and ignore the IV order
Wait until the next scheduled equipment round

questions.rationale: The nurse must treat the alarm as a potential patient safety event. Both patient assessment and equipment correction are essential.

questions.title: Advanced decision
questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Verify infusion orders, settings, and line patency
Document the event and patient response accurately
Report defective or unreliable equipment if relevant
Reflect on alarm fatigue and prevention strategies with the team
Assume alarms are harmless if the patient is asleep

questions.rationale: All of these are correct. Safe equipment use includes clear documentation, order verification, and reporting of malfunction or workflow issues.

questions.title: Evaluate outcomes
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective management?

options.text: The patient is reassessed promptly, the infusion problem is corrected, and the equipment issue is not ignored again
Alarms continue to be silenced without review
Documentation omits the incident
The patient worsens while staff assume the pump is fine

questions.rationale: Effective management involves rapid correction, patient reassessment, and prevention of repeated unsafe alarm responses.
